blocks.text: the old Scholiast says: He referred "doves" to simplicity. And in the Suda ἡμένη πελειὰς [hēmenē peleias], a sitting dove, is used as a proverb ἐπὶ τῶν ἁπλουστάτων [epi tōn haploustatōn], of the most simple-minded. This is, of course, διὰ τὸ εὔηθες τοῦ ζώου [dia to euēthes tou zōou], because of the creature's stupidity, as Eustathius has it on Iliad ψ΄ [psi]. The proverb, however, is not used of every dove, but of those that sit beside the decoy dove. As the Suda says, it is κατὰ ἀντιπαρεξέτασιν τῆς παλευτρίας [kata antiparexetasin tēs paleutrias], by contrast with the decoy dove, that is, the dove that fowlers misuse to lure the others. Aristophanes in the Birds:
Τὰς περιστερὰς θ᾽ ὁμοίως ξυλλαβὼν εἵρξας ἔχει Κἀπαναγκάζει παλεύειν δεδεμένας ἐν δικτύῳ· [Tas peristeras th' homoiōs xyllabōn heirxas echei / Kapanankazei paleuein dedemenas en diktyō]

And likewise he seizes the doves, keeps them confined, and forces them, bound in a net, to lure others. And there the Scholiast says: Εἰώθασιν ἐκτυφλοῦντές τινα τῶν ὀρνέων ἱστάναι ἐν δικτύῳ, ὅπως τῇ φωνῇ προσκαλεῖτο τὰ ὁμοιογενῆ· [Eiōthasin ektyphlountes tina tōn orneōn histanai en diktyō, hopōs tē phōnē proskaleito ta homoiogenē] They are accustomed to keep a blinded bird in a snare, so that by its voice it may call others of its kind. That doves were used for this purpose is asserted not only by Aristophanes but also by the Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 7: Αἱ περισταὶ, he says, ζῶσι καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη, αἱ τετυφλωμέναι ὑπὸ τῶν παλευτρίας τρεφόντων αὐτάς· [Hai peristerai … zōsi kai oktō etē, hai tetyphlōmenai hypo tōn paleutrias trephontōn autas] Doves that are blinded and kept as decoys live as long as eight years. Now, if you consult more recent writers, what has been said about the simplicity of doves and the ease of catching them will be considerably confirmed by what [II, 553] Cadamosto relates happened to him, Navigat. ch. 40, when he first landed on the Canary Islands. The doves, he says, were caught at will by a man's hand. For they were not frightened at the sight of a man. And in chapter 6, on the island of Madeira: I remember hearing from the inhabitants that when the island was first settled there was a very great abundance of doves there. To catch them the fowlers used no other device than a hook tied to a pole, so that they might be drawn to them from the trees on which they perch there; the birds were not frightened but full of wonder, as at something never seen before.

Meanwhile, those who take ἀκεραίους [akeraious] in Christ's saying to mean mild and gentle have followed a good many Grammarians, for whom ἀκέραιον [akeraion], said of an animal, means hornless, as well as kindly and harmless. Beyond this, they have had regard to the nature of the dove, which is in truth a most mild and gentle animal. Accordingly Ovid calls it placid, Metam. book 7, Fable 12. And Cyril says that the dove πρὸς ἄκρον ἥκειν πρᾳότητος [pros akron hēkein praotētos], reaches the highest summit of gentleness, in book 15 On Adoration. Indeed, many think it entirely lacks gall. Hence Clement calls it ἄχολον [acholon], Paedag. book 1, ch. 5; and Isidore, Orig. book 12, calls doves gentle birds without gall. Of the same kind is what Tertullian writes, On Baptism ch. 8, that the dove, even bodily, lacks gall itself. And Sedulius, book 2 of the Carmen, on the Baptism of Christ:
And it befits the Gentle One, the greatly Mild, to come forth through the bird that lacks gall. — —

And Horapollo, Hieroglyph. book 1, ch. 54: Ἱστορεῖται δὲ ὅτι οὐ χολὴν ἔχει τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον [Historeitai de hoti ou cholēn echei touto to zōon], It is also reported that this animal lacks gall. Yet he himself refutes this in book 2, ch. 45, saying that the dove ἐν ὀπισθίοις τὴν χολὴν ἔχειν [en opisthiois tēn cholēn echein], has its gall at the back. And Galen, in the book On Black Bile, says those people are ridiculous who think the dove lacks gall because it does not have τὴν ἐπὶ τῷ ἤπατι κύστιν [tēn epi tō hēpati kystin], the gall bladder next to the liver. Nor did this escape the Philosopher, whose words are, Hist. book 2, ch. 15: Ἔνιοι πρὸς τῇ κοιλίᾳ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ πρὸς τοῖς ἐντέροις τὴν χολὴν, οἷον περιστερά [Enioi pros tē koilia echousin, hoi de pros tois enterois tēn cholēn, hoion peristera]. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 37: In some the gall is attached only to the intestine, as in doves.

Another point to be noted here in doves is their conjugal chastity, which the ancients praise remarkably. Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 7: Οὔτε γὰρ συν- [col. 23] δυάζεσθαι θέλουσι πλείοσιν, οὔτε προσλείπουσι τὴν κοινωνίαν, πλὴν ἐὰν χῆρος, ἢ χήρα γένηται· [Oute gar syndyazesthai thelousi pleiosin, oute proleipousi tēn koinōnian, plēn ean chēros ē chēra genētai] For they will not pair with more than one, nor do they ever abandon their partnership, except through widowhood. Pliny, book 10, ch. 34: Chastity is foremost with them, and adultery is known to neither. They do not violate conjugal fidelity, and they keep a common home. Unless unmated or widowed, a dove does not leave its nest. Propertius, book 2, Eleg. 12:
[II, 554] So let doves joined in love be my example, male and female, a whole marriage.
